Tutorial 8: Gridded Climate and Environmental Data

climasus4r Team

20/09/2026

Source: vignettes/08-clima-grade.Rmd
08-clima-grade.Rmd

Objective

By the end of this tutorial you will be able to integrate gridded climate and environmental data (remote sensing and reanalysis) into your health time series: import ERA5-Land (~10 km) with sus_grid_era5() and aggregate it to municipal polygons; get to know the full sus_grid_* family (CHIRPS precipitation, fire hotspots, PDSI/SMVI droughts, PRODES deforestation, and CAMS/GHAP/MERRA-2 pollution); and derive climate indicators for epidemiology: anomalies (sus_climate_anomaly()), bioclimatic indices (sus_climate_compute_indicators()), heatwaves (sus_climate_compute_heatwaves() + sus_climate_plot_heatwaves()), and the drought indices SPI (sus_climate_compute_spi()) and SPEI (sus_climate_compute_spei()).

This is the eighth stage of the pipeline: while Tutorial 7 built the climate exposure from INMET stations (point measurements), here we build an alternative and complementary gridded exposure — continuous spatial coverage, with no observation gaps — that will feed the DLNM model in Tutorial 9.

Scientific context

Station vs. pixel: two ways of measuring exposure

A weather station measures climate at a point; a gridded product represents the mean value of a pixel (a fixed-area cell). ERA5-Land (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021) is a reanalysis: a physical land-surface model driven by observations, producing continuous hourly fields since 1950 at ~0.1° resolution (~10 km at the equator). For Brazil, the ERA5-Land Daily Aggregates for Latin America project (Saldanha, Zenodo, CC-BY 4.0) provides ready-made daily aggregates, requiring no API key — this is the source used by sus_grid_era5().

Three caveats for anyone working with remote sensing/reanalysis:

  1. Resolution and representativeness. A ~10 km pixel is an areal average: it smooths out local extremes (urban heat islands, valley microclimates) that a point station would capture. On the other hand, it covers municipalities without a station and has no missing data. For a large municipality such as São Paulo (~1,500 km²), dozens of pixels are aggregated to the polygon — climasus4r does this with an area-weighted mean of the intersection (via exactextractr), which avoids edge bias.
  2. Physical units. The original NetCDF files come in SI units: temperature in Kelvin (K → °C conversion: subtract 273.15), precipitation in meters (m → mm: multiply by 1,000), and pressure in Pa (Pa → hPa: divide by 100). sus_grid_era5() applies these conversions automatically and delivers canonical columns (tair_dry_bulb_c, rainfall_mm, …).
  3. Cross-validation. Reanalysis does not replace observation: it is recommended to compare the gridded series with the nearest INMET station (Tutorial 7) before choosing the model’s exposure — systematic differences (bias) are expected and should be documented.

From raw fields to epidemiological indicators

The climate-health literature rarely uses raw temperature directly:

  • Anomalies (WMO, 2017) make cities with different climates comparable and highlight extreme days to correlate with mortality peaks (Gasparrini et al., 2017);
  • Heatwaves defined by percentiles and duration (Perkins & Alexander, 2013; Geirinhas et al., 2018) and by the Excess Heat Factor — EHF (Nairn & Fawcett, 2015) capture the acute effect of sustained heat;
  • SPI (McKee et al., 1993) and SPEI (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010) standardize drought/wetness across multiple time scales — relevant to diarrheal diseases, leptospirosis, and arboviral diseases;
  • Bioclimatic indices (UTCI, Bröde et al., 2012; WBGT, Liljegren et al., 2008; HI, Rothfusz, 1990) combine temperature, humidity, wind, and radiation into a single measure of human thermal stress.

Guiding case. We continue with temperature and health outcomes in older adults (60+) in the São Paulo Metropolitan Region, 2014–2019. In this tutorial we import ERA5-Land for the municipality of São Paulo and derive anomalies, heatwaves, and SPI/SPEI. The result (caso_clima_grade.rds) feeds into Tutorial 9 as an alternative/ complementary exposure to the station-based one (caso_clima_estacao.rds, Tutorial 7).

Data used

Source Function Resolution Variables Role in the case
ERA5-Land (Zenodo) sus_grid_era5() ~10 km, daily Mean, max, min temperature, precipitation Primary gridded exposure
Health series (T4) dados/caso_serie.rds Municipality × day Deaths J00–J99/I00–I99, 60+ Temporal/spatial skeleton

Chained input: dados/caso_serie.rds (Tutorial 4). Output: dados/caso_clima_grade.rds (a list with the ERA5-Land daily series, the aligned health+climate series, monthly SPI/SPEI, and the heatwave events).

The sus_grid_* family covers other environmental sources with the same grammar (years/months, municipalities as an sf object, pixel→polygon aggregation, caching):

Function Source Theme
sus_grid_chirps() CHIRPS (0.05°) Precipitation (Funk et al., 2015)
sus_grid_fires() INPE/Queimadas Fire hotspots
sus_grid_pdsi() PDSI Drought (Palmer index)
sus_grid_smvi() SMVI Flash drought (soil moisture)
sus_grid_prodes() PRODES/TerraBrasilis Deforestation
sus_grid_pollution_cams() CAMS/Copernicus Air pollution (reanalysis)
sus_grid_pollution_ghap() GHAP High-resolution PM2.5
sus_grid_pollution_merra2() MERRA-2/NASA Aerosols and pollutants
sus_grid_join() — Joins grids to the health base by code_muni × date

Full pipeline

The blocks below reproduce what scripts/tutorial_08_clima_grade.R executes. Start by loading the package and the chained health series:

library(climasus4r)

caso_serie <- readRDS("dados/caso_serie.rds")  # série diária de saúde (T4)

Importing ERA5-Land for the municipality of São Paulo

First we obtain the municipal polygon (an sf object via geobr) and then call sus_grid_era5(). The function downloads the NetCDF files from Zenodo (no API key needed), converts units (K → °C; m → mm), and aggregates each pixel to the polygon with an area-weighted mean:

library(geobr)

sp_geom <- read_municipality(code_muni = "SP", year = 2020)
sp_geom <- sp_geom[as.character(sp_geom$code_muni) == "3550308", ]  # São Paulo

era5_sp <- sus_grid_era5(
  years          = 2014:2019,
  months         = 1:12,
  vars           = c("t2m", "t2m_max", "t2m_min", "tp"),
  municipalities = sp_geom,    # sf -> agrega raster ao polígono
  agg_fun        = "mean",     # média areal (ponderada) do município
  use_cache      = TRUE,       # NetCDF reaproveitados em ~/.climasus4r_cache/era5
  parallel       = FALSE,
  lang           = "pt",
  verbose        = TRUE
)

sus_meta(era5_sp, "stage")  # "climate"
sus_meta(era5_sp, "type")   # "era5_land"

The return value is a climasus_df with code_muni, date, and one column per variable: tair_dry_bulb_c (t2m), tair_max_c (t2m_max), tair_min_c (t2m_min), and rainfall_mm (tp).

Climate anomalies

sus_climate_anomaly() compares observations to INMET’s climatological normals (from sus_climate_normals()), with three methods — absolute, relative, and standardized:

normais <- sus_climate_normals(
  period     = "1991-2020",
  target_var = c("t_max", "t_min", "t_mean_comp", "precipitation")
)

anom <- sus_climate_anomaly(
  observed   = clima_estacao,        # climasus_df do T7 (estações INMET)
  normals    = normais,
  method     = "standardized",       # z-score: comparável entre cidades
  time_scale = "monthly",
  lang       = "pt"
)

Since the ERA5-Land series uses code_muni (rather than station_code matched to the INMET normals), the generation script illustrates the same mathematics using the monthly climatology derived from the series itself — obs − month mean and the corresponding z-score (see the formulas below).

Bioclimatic indicators (demonstration)

sus_climate_compute_indicators() computes WBGT, HI, THI, UTCI, PET, degree-days (CDD/HDD/GDD), and others, from hourly data with temperature, humidity (rh_mean_porc), radiation (sr_kj_m2), and wind (ws_2_m_s):

clima_ind <- sus_climate_compute_indicators(
  df         = clima_horario,                  # T7 (INMET horário) ou ERA5 com td2m/u10/v10/sp
  indicators = c("wbgt", "hi", "utci"),
  region     = "atlantic_forest",              # limiares adaptados ao bioma
  lang       = "pt"
)

The minimal ERA5-Land series used in this tutorial (temperature and rain only) does not carry humidity/wind/radiation; in a real workflow, apply the function to the hourly INMET series (T7) or request vars = "all" in sus_grid_era5() (includes td2m, u10, v10, sp).

Heatwaves

sus_climate_compute_heatwaves() expects a climasus_df at stage = "climate" with date, station_code, and temperature columns. We adapt the gridded series to this contract (station_code = code_muni) and apply three methods:

hw <- sus_climate_compute_heatwaves(
  df             = era5_hw,                   # ERA5 adaptado ao contrato de estação
  method         = c("WHO", "WMO", "INMET"),  # ou "all" (inclui EHF, UTCI, WBGT, HI)
  baseline_start = "2014-01-01",              # período de referência dos percentis
  baseline_end   = "2019-12-31",
  percentile     = 90,                        # P90 para WHO/WMO
  lang           = "pt"
)

hw$events    # um evento por linha: início, fim, duração, pico, intensidade
hw$daily     # flags diárias hw_who, hw_wmo, hw_inmet, hw_any
hw$summary   # resumo anual por estação e método

A ready-made visualization comes from sus_climate_plot_heatwaves():

sus_climate_plot_heatwaves(
  hw,
  type        = "trend",     # ou "timeline", "calendar", "intensity"
  interactive = FALSE,       # TRUE -> plotly
  lang        = "pt"
)

SPI and SPEI: droughts and wet periods

Both functions require monthly data (one row per municipality × month, with date on the 1st day of the month). We aggregate the daily series: precipitation by sum, temperature by mean:

mensal <- era5_sp |>
  dplyr::mutate(date_m = as.Date(format(date, "%Y-%m-01"))) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    rainfall_mm     = sum(rainfall_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    tair_dry_bulb_c = mean(tair_dry_bulb_c, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c("code_muni", "date_m")
  ) |>
  dplyr::rename(date = date_m)

# SPI: apenas precipitação (gamma + zeros)
spi <- sus_climate_compute_spi(
  df     = mensal,
  var    = "rainfall_mm",        # padrão é "rainfall_chirps_mm" (sus_grid_chirps)
  scales = c(1L, 3L, 6L),        # série de 6 anos: escalas curtas
  min_n  = 24L,                  # mínimo de 24 meses para ajustar a distribuição
  lang   = "pt"
)

# SPEI: balanço hídrico P - PET (PET de Thornthwaite, só temperatura)
spei <- sus_climate_compute_spei(
  df         = spi,
  rain_var   = "rainfall_mm",
  pet_method = "thornthwaite",   # ou "column" com pet_var = "pet_mm"
  temp_var   = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  scales     = c(1L, 3L, 6L),
  min_n      = 24L,
  lang       = "pt"
)

names(spei)  # ..., spi_1mo, spi_3mo, spi_6mo, spei_1mo, spei_3mo, spei_6mo

Methodological note. The WMO recommends ≥ 30 years of calibration for SPI/SPEI (ref_start/ref_end). With 6 years (72 months), the indices in this case are illustrative: in real research, calibrate with CHIRPS 1981–2010 (sus_grid_chirps()) or ERA5-Land since 1950.

Chaining: aligning gridded climate to health and saving for T9

Finally, we join the daily ERA5-Land temperature to the health series by date and save the gridded exposure bundle that Tutorial 9 will use:

saude_clima <- dplyr::left_join(
  caso_serie,
  era5_sp |> dplyr::select(date, tair_dry_bulb_c, tair_max_c,
                           tair_min_c, rainfall_mm),
  by = "date"
)

caso_clima_grade <- list(
  era5_diario = era5_sp,
  saude_clima = saude_clima,
  spi_spei    = spei,
  ondas_calor = hw$events
)
saveRDS(caso_clima_grade, "dados/caso_clima_grade.rds")

Function characteristics

sus_grid_era5()

The entry point for ERA5-Land: downloads daily aggregates from Zenodo (Saldanha, 1950–2025) and aggregates pixels to municipal polygons.

Argument Essential? Description
years yes Years (1950–2025), e.g. 2014:2019
months optional Months 1–12 (default: all)
vars optional ERA5 aliases: "t2m", "t2m_max", "t2m_min", "td2m", "u10", "v10", "sp", "tp", or "all" (default c("t2m","tp"))
municipalities recommended sf object with the polygons (detects code_muni/CD_MUN); NULL returns only the NetCDF paths
agg_fun optional Pixel→polygon aggregation via exactextractr: "mean" (default, area-weighted), "sum", "median", "min", "max"
use_cache / cache_dir recommended Reuses downloaded NetCDF files (~/.climasus4r_cache/era5)
parallel / workers optional Parallel downloads; respects the user’s future::plan()
lang / verbose optional Language ("pt", "en", "es") and messages

Return: climasus_df [stage = "climate", type = "era5_land"] with code_muni, date, and canonical columns already in practical units (tair_dry_bulb_c in °C, rainfall_mm in mm, patm_hpa in hPa).

sus_climate_anomaly()

Argument Description
observed climasus_df from sus_climate_inmet() or sus_climate_aggregate()
normals climasus_df from sus_climate_normals() (columns codigo, mes, decada, var_code, valor)
vars Map of observed column → normals var_code, e.g. c(tair_max_c = "t_max"); NULL auto-detects
method "absolute" (default), "relative", "standardized", or "all"
time_scale "monthly" (default) or "decadal" (10-day periods)
station_col / date_col Names of the station and date columns ("station_code", "date")

Return: climasus_df [stage = "climate", type = "anomaly"], one row per station × year × month, with {v}_obs, {v}_normal, {v}_anomaly, and, depending on the method, {v}_anomaly_pct and {v}_anomaly_std.

sus_climate_compute_indicators()

Argument Description
df Hourly data from sus_climate_inmet()/sus_climate_fill_inmet()
indicators "all" (default) or codes: "wbgt", "hi", "thi", "wcet", "wct", "et", "utci", "pet", "cdd", "hdd", "gdd", "diurnal_range", "vapor_pressure", "heat_stress_risk", "koppen_humidity"
region "auto" (default) or biome: "amazon", "cerrado", "caatinga", "atlantic_forest", "pampa", "pantanal", "southeast", "south"
confidence_flags _flag_extreme/_flag_high/_flag_low flags per indicator
verify_physics Checks solar radiation against extraterrestrial limits
compute_uncertainty 95% CI via Monte Carlo (200 simulations)

Return: climasus_df with columns such as wbgt_c, hi_c, utci_c — a prerequisite for the UTCI/WBGT/HI heatwave methods.

sus_climate_compute_heatwaves()

Argument Description
df climasus_df [stage="climate", type inmet/filled/indicators] with date, station_code, and temperatures
method "WHO", "WMO", "INMET", "EHF", "UTCI", "WBGT", "HI", or "all" (methods missing a required column are skipped with a warning)
baseline_start / baseline_end Reference period for the thresholds; NULL uses the whole series
percentile Threshold percentile (default 90)
min_duration Minimum consecutive days; NULL uses each method’s default (WHO=3, WMO=5, INMET=5, EHF=3…)

Return: a climasus_hw list with events (discrete events), daily (daily flags hw_<method>, hw_any), and summary (annual summary). Visualization via sus_climate_plot_heatwaves(hw_result, type = "timeline" | "calendar" | "intensity" | "trend", interactive, lang).

sus_climate_compute_spi() and sus_climate_compute_spei()

Argument SPI SPEI
df monthly, with code_muni + date same
rainfall variable var (default "rainfall_chirps_mm") rain_var
PET — pet_method = "column" (pet_var) or "thornthwaite" (temp_var)
scales scales in months (default c(1,3,6,12)) same
ref_start / ref_end calibration period (WMO: ≥ 30 years) same
min_n minimum valid months per municipality (default 24) same

Return: the input climasus_df with columns spi_{s}mo / spei_{s}mo (type = "spi" / "spei"). Distributions: gamma with a zero-inflation mixture (SPI); 3-parameter log-logistic via L-moments (SPEI).

Formulas

Anomaly (WMO, 2017). For variable xx in month mm of year tt, with climatological normal x‾m\bar{x}_m and interannual standard deviation σm\sigma_m:

At,m=xt,m−x‾m(absolute, °C) A_{t,m} = x_{t,m} - \bar{x}_m \qquad\text{(absolute, °C)}

Zt,m=xt,m−x‾mσm(standardized, z-score) Z_{t,m} = \frac{x_{t,m} - \bar{x}_m}{\sigma_m} \qquad\text{(standardized, z-score)}

The "relative" method divides by |x‾m||\bar{x}_m| and multiplies by 100 (%, customary for precipitation).

SPI (McKee et al., 1993). Precipitation accumulated over ss months, PsP_s, is fitted to a gamma distribution (with probability p0p_0 of dry months) and transformed to the standard normal:

SPIs=Φ−1[p0+(1−p0)Fγ(Ps)] \mathrm{SPI}_s = \Phi^{-1}\!\big[\, p_0 + (1 - p_0)\, F_\gamma(P_s)\,\big]

where FγF_\gamma is the gamma CDF and Φ−1\Phi^{-1} the inverse standard normal. Values ≤−1\le -1 indicate moderate drought; ≤−1,5\le -1{,}5 severe; ≤−2\le -2 extreme.

SPEI (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010). Replaces PP with the accumulated climatic water balance, sensitive to warming:

D=P−PET,SPEIs=Φ−1[FLL(∑sD)] D = P - \mathrm{PET}, \qquad \mathrm{SPEI}_s = \Phi^{-1}\!\big[\, F_{LL}\!\big(\textstyle\sum_s D\big)\,\big]

with FLLF_{LL} the 3-parameter log-logistic CDF and PET estimated by Thornthwaite (1948) when only temperature is available.

EHF — Excess Heat Factor (Nairn & Fawcett, 2015). Combines the anomaly against the climate (EHIsig\mathrm{EHI}_{sig}) and against the recent 30 days (acclimatization, EHIacc\mathrm{EHI}_{acc}):

EHIsig=T‾3−T95,EHIacc=T‾3−T‾30 \mathrm{EHI}_{sig} = \bar{T}_3 - T_{95}, \qquad \mathrm{EHI}_{acc} = \bar{T}_3 - \bar{T}_{30}

EHF=EHIsig×max⁡(1,EHIacc) \mathrm{EHF} = \mathrm{EHI}_{sig} \times \max(1,\ \mathrm{EHI}_{acc})

where T‾3\bar{T}_3 and T‾30\bar{T}_{30} are the means of TmeanT_{mean} over the last 3 and 30 days, and T95T_{95} is the 95th percentile of the baseline. The WHO/WMO methods, in turn, require Tmax>P90(Tmax)T_{max} > P_{90}(T_{max}) (WMO also Tmin>P90(Tmin)T_{min} > P_{90}(T_{min})) for a minimum number of consecutive days.

Figure 1. Mean daily temperature from ERA5-Land (~10 km) aggregated to the municipality of São Paulo, 2014–2019. Note the typical smoothness of the areal value: averaging dozens of pixels dampens the local extremes a station would record — this is the trade-off for complete spatial coverage.

Figure 2. Monthly temperature anomaly (observed − monthly normal), São Paulo, 2014–2019. Orange bars (positive) mark months warmer than the local climatology; it is exactly this signal — rather than the absolute temperature — that travels between cities in multicenter analyses.

Figure 3. Heatwaves detected per year and method (WHO/WMO/INMET) in the São Paulo ERA5-Land series, 2014–2019. More demanding methods (WMO: dual threshold on Tmax and Tmin for ≥ 5 days) detect fewer events than the WHO criterion (P90 of Tmax for ≥ 3 days) — the choice should reflect the physiological mechanism of interest (daytime heat vs. warm nights without relief).

Artefato indisponível — rode Rscript scripts/tutorial_08_clima_grade.R (a partir da raiz do pacote) para gerá-lo.

Figure 4. Monthly SPI-3 vs. SPEI-3 (dashed lines: ±1 = moderate threshold). When temperature rises without a change in rainfall, SPEI drops more than SPI — potential evapotranspiration amplifies the water deficit. São Paulo’s 2014–2015 water crisis is the kind of episode these indices signal ahead of time for outcomes such as diarrheal diseases.
